cases.note: METHODOLOGY 3.1 - a date spine is the correct construction for a dense calendar, not a defect. Firing here is an FP.
METHODOLOGY 3.2 - SELECT * inside a CTE is acceptable; only a final projection SELECT * is a finding. The final projection here is explicit.
METHODOLOGY 3.3 - the author intends to drop payments with no customer. Firing is an FP.
METHODOLOGY 3.4 - countries is a <500-row reference table; an unfiltered scan is correct.
METHODOLOGY 3.5 - the reference-correct fix for a fan-out. The detector is right to stay silent; firing is an FP.
Pre-ANSI-92 join syntax, correctly related in WHERE. Regression guard for the comma-join detection added after Phase 1.
NOT IN is only dangerous over a nullable column. countries.code is a NOT NULL primary key, so this is safe.
ORDER BY carries a unique tie-breaker, so row numbering is stable.
Numerator cast to numeric and denominator NULLIF-guarded: neither truncation nor divide-by-zero applies.
COUNT(*) is only misleading after a child join. There is no join here.
The CTE looks like pre-aggregation but does not aggregate - it joins. The SUM outside is still inflated.
The comment claims the LEFT JOIN is preserved, but the WHERE predicate on the right side silently converts it to an INNER JOIN.
The = NULL is buried in an OR branch and looks like a null check.
The WHERE inside the subquery looks protective but does not exclude NULL customer_id, so NOT IN can still collapse to zero rows.
Wrapping an integer division in AVG does not stop the truncation - each row truncates to 0 or 1 before averaging.
Two CTEs make it look disciplined, but the final projection is SELECT * over the whole chain.
COALESCE in the ON clause reads as defensive null handling but silently inflates matches and defeats the index.
ORDER BY created_at looks deterministic but DATE has day granularity, so same-day customers tie and order arbitrarily.
Aliasing to cust/sub makes cust.id = sub.id read like a real relationship. It joins two unrelated surrogate keys.
churn_risk_score is exactly the sort of column an LLM invents: plausible, domain-appropriate, and not in the schema.
